run.question: Debug memory issues for my Python application orca in namespace app-95

report.summary: I fetched runbook skill_id python-memory-troubleshooting and carried out its steps with my own tools: (1) application status — one pod, orca-57fdcbf45f-svctq in namespace app-95, is Running but its orca container's last termination was OOMKilled with exit code 137 (started 16:44:53Z, finished 16:45:23Z) and restartCount 1; no kubelet OOMKilling/Evicted event was returned; (2) logs — the previous container and the restarted one both log an unbounded retention pattern: startup says 'Configuration: Storing all processed images for audit trail' and 'Configuration: Caching thumbnails for quick retrieval', then repeats 'Cache size: N thumbnails', 'processed_images list has N items' and 'Approximate memory used by stored images', rising 22.8 MB (20 images) → 110.7 MB (90 images) before the OOM at image 100; (3) code patterns — the memory is held in an ever-growing thumbnail cache and processed_images list, ~1.3 MB per image, with no eviction visible; (4) growth pattern — the new container restarted at 16:45:24Z and reproduced the same growth (64.0 MB at 50 images by 16:45:29Z); (5) limits — Deployment orca sets container orca memory limit 128Mi / request 64Mi, image python:3.9-slim, env only PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 and SERVICE_NAME=orca-image-processor, and the only ConfigMap in the namespace is kube-root-ca.crt, so no cache-bound setting exists outside the image. Prometheus was unreachable (SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE on three attempts), so no memory-metric series or alert-rule check could be made; that is a gap, not zero. The deepest cause supported is unbounded in-process retention hitting the 128Mi container limit defined in Deployment orca, so the pod was OOMKilled and will recur on the same trajectory.

claims.text: Pod orca-57fdcbf45f-svctq in namespace app-95 is Running, owned by ReplicaSet orca-57fdcbf45f, and its container 'orca' has restartCount 1 with lastState.terminated.reason = OOMKilled and exitCode 137, startedAt 2026-11-23T16:44:53Z, finishedAt 2026-11-23T16:45:23Z; the current instance has been running since 2026-11-23T16:45:24Z.

Deployment orca (namespace app-95) defines exactly one container 'orca' with image python:3.9-slim, resources limits memory 128Mi and requests cpu 10m / memory 64Mi, env PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 and SERVICE_NAME=orca-image-processor; generation is 1 and it was last updated by kubectl-client-side-apply at 2026-11-23T16:44:52Z, with 1/1 replicas available and ready.

The previous (OOMKilled) orca container logged 'Configuration: Storing all processed images for audit trail' and 'Configuration: Caching thumbnails for quick retrieval', then repeatedly logged 'Cache size: N thumbnails', 'Memory usage: processed_images list has N items' and 'Approximate memory used by stored images', growing from 22.8 MB at 20 items (16:44:55Z) to 110.7 MB at 90 items (16:45:18Z); the last line was 'Processing image 100' at 16:45:23.944Z, immediately before the container terminated.

The restarted orca container reproduced the same growth in the same pod: it logged 'Cache size: 50 thumbnails' and 'Approximate memory used by stored images: 64.0 MB' at 16:45:29.587Z, following the prior container's ~1.3 MB-per-image trajectory toward the 128Mi limit.

The only ConfigMap present in namespace app-95 is kube-root-ca.crt, i.e. no application ConfigMap carries cache-size, retention or memory settings for orca; the memory-related configuration observed is only the startup log lines emitted by the application itself.

Events in namespace app-95 in the window show Deployment orca ScalingReplicaSet (replica set orca-57fdcbf45f scaled 0→1 at 16:44:52Z), ReplicaSet orca-57fdcbf45f SuccessfulCreate 'Created pod: orca-57fdcbf45f-svctq', and Pod orca-57fdcbf45f-svctq Scheduled, Created, Pulled and Started (Created/Pulled/Started count 2, last 16:45:24Z); no event in the returned set carries reason OOMKilling or Evicted for this pod.
Exactly one pod matching 'orca' exists cluster-wide: app-95/orca-57fdcbf45f-svctq, phase Running (33 pods processed in the query).

ReplicaSet orca-57fdcbf45f is owned by Deployment orca with annotation deployment.kubernetes.io/revision=1, was created 2026-11-23T16:44:52Z, and has 1 desired / 1 ready / 1 available replica on image python:3.9-slim.

Primary hypothesis: the orca process retains every processed image in memory (thumbnail cache plus a processed_images list kept 'for audit trail') with no eviction, growing about 1.3 MB per image, which exhausts the container's 128Mi memory limit defined in Deployment orca and causes the kubelet to kill it with OOMKilled/137 roughly every 100 images; the cycle repeats on each restart because nothing bounds the caches.

Node-level memory pressure / eviction is rejected as the termination mechanism: the container's own last termination reason is OOMKilled with exit code 137, the pod was not recreated (same pod name and uid, restartCount 1, same node opspilot-m1-control-plane), and no Evicted-reason event was returned for it.

A rolling rollout of a changed pod template is rejected as the trigger: Deployment orca is generation 1 with a single ReplicaSet annotation revision=1 created at 16:44:52Z, so the 16:45:23Z interruption was an in-place container restart of the same pod, not a new pod from a template change.

Bound the retention: cap or TTL the thumbnail cache (e.g. functools.lru_cache(maxsize=...) or an OrderedDict with eviction) and the processed_images list (collections.deque(maxlen=...) or stop storing images after the audit metadata), or make the 'audit trail' setting write to disk instead of keeping full images in RAM.

If full in-memory retention is intended, raise Deployment orca's container memory limit well above the observed peak (110.7 MB was reached at 90 images and still climbing) and keep the request aligned; but note this only defers the OOM because growth is linear and unbounded.

Add profiling/alerting the runbook suggests: enable tracemalloc or attach py-spy (if present in the image) to confirm the retained objects, and alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes / OOMKilled restarts for app-95/orca once Prometheus scraping is reachable.

gaps: Prometheus was unreachable for this Run: get_metric_names, get_all_labels and execute_prometheus_instant_query all returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so container memory working-set series, OOMKilled/restart counters and alert-rule state for app-95/orca are unknown rather than zero.

The application source and container image contents (python:3.9-slim plus the mounted orca code) cannot be read; which in-process structure retains the images and whether any eviction code exists is inferred only from the application's own log lines.

Only 220 log lines were kept by the node and the newest 200 were shown (16 lines lay outside the read window); log history before 2026-11-23T16:44:54Z and after 2026-11-23T16:45:35Z is unknown, so earlier OOM cycles cannot be excluded.
No kubelet OOMKilling event was returned for this pod; the OOM is known from the container's lastState (OOMKilled, exit code 137) rather than an event.

Secrets and the Deployment's full pod-template history before 16:44:52Z are unavailable (no change-history integration is configured), so whether the 128Mi limit or the retention behaviour was changed earlier could not be checked.
Downstream/user impact of the orca restarts is not observable here (no traces for orca in the available service list, and no request metrics reachable); it remains unverified.
next_steps: Confirm with a memory profile inside the pod (py-spy dump or tracemalloc in the app) that the thumbnail cache and processed_images list are the growing objects, and measure steady-state size.
Patch the application to bound or offload the cache/audit store, then verify memory stays flat across several hundred images.
Restore Prometheus scraping and add an alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes and on container OOMKilled restarts for app-95/orca so the next growth cycle is caught before the kill.

# Python Application Memory Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose memory issues in Python applications running in Kubernetes.

## Investigation Steps

### 1. Check Application Status
Check if the application pods are running and review recent events:
```bash
kubectl get pods -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}
kubectl describe pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}
kubectl top pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}
```

### 2. Review Application Logs
Look for memory errors, GC warnings, or memory-related messages:
```bash
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} --tail=100 | grep -E "(memory|Memory|ERROR|WARNING|GC|Cache|processed)"
```

Pay attention to:
- Processing patterns and batch sizes
- Cache growth indicators
- Memory allocation patterns

### 3. Analyze Application Code Patterns
Look for common memory leak patterns in logs:
```bash
# Check for growing collections or caches
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -E "size:|count:|total:|cache"

# Look for processing patterns
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -E "Processing|processed|Batch"
```

Common memory leak indicators:
- Continuously growing collections (lists, dicts)
- Caches without eviction policies
- Circular references preventing garbage collection

### 4. Identify Memory Growth Patterns
Analyze how memory usage correlates with application activity:
```bash
# Monitor memory growth over time
kubectl top pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} --use-protocol-buffers

# Correlate with processing activity
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} --tail=50
```

### 5. Monitor Memory Metrics
Check memory usage patterns over time:
```bash
# Get current memory usage
kubectl top pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name}

# Review resource limits
kubectl describe pod -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -A3 "Limits:"
```

## Python-Specific Memory Profiling

### Using Built-in Tools
If the application has profiling endpoints or debug mode:
```bash
# Check if app exposes memory profiling endpoints
kubectl exec -n {namespace} {pod_name} -- curl localhost:8000/debug/memory 2>/dev/null || echo "No debug endpoint"

# If the app uses Flask/Django debug toolbar
kubectl port-forward -n {namespace} {pod_name} 8000:8000
# Then visit http://localhost:8000/debug
```

### Memory Profiling with py-spy (if available in container)
```bash
# Check if py-spy is installed
kubectl exec -n {namespace} {pod_name} -- which py-spy

# If available, profile the running process
kubectl exec -n {namespace} {pod_name} -- py-spy dump --pid 1
```

### Using tracemalloc (if enabled in code)
Look for tracemalloc output in logs:
```bash
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -E "tracemalloc|Top.*memory blocks"
```

### Memory Usage Patterns
Check for memory allocation patterns in logs:
```bash
# Look for object creation patterns
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -E "Created|Allocated|New.*object"

# Check garbage collection activity
kubectl logs -n {namespace} -l app={app_name} | grep -E "gc\.|GC|garbage"
```

## Common Python Memory Leak Patterns

1. **Unbounded Collections**: Lists/dicts that grow without limits
   - Solution: Implement size limits or use collections.deque with maxlen
   - Profile: Look for growing collection sizes in logs

2. **Cache Without Eviction**: Caching data without removing old entries
   - Solution: Use functools.lru_cache or implement TTL-based eviction
   - Profile: Monitor cache size metrics in logs

3. **Keeping References to Large Objects**: Storing processed data unnecessarily
   - Solution: Process and discard, use generators for streaming
   - Profile: Check for accumulating processed items

4. **Global State Accumulation**: Module-level variables that accumulate data
   - Solution: Encapsulate in classes with proper cleanup
   - Profile: Look for module-level collections in stack traces

5. **Circular References**: Objects referencing each other preventing GC
   - Solution: Use weakref for one direction of the reference
   - Profile: Check for objects with high reference counts

6. **Large Object Allocation**: Creating unnecessarily large objects
   - Solution: Process data in chunks, use numpy arrays for numerical data
   - Profile: Look for large allocation warnings or patterns

query.jq_expr: .items[] | {name: .metadata.name, phase: .status.phase, owner: .metadata.ownerReferences, containers: [.status.containerStatuses[]? | {name, ready, restartCount, lastState: .lastState, state: .state}], limits: [.spec.containers[] | {name, resources: .resources}], node: .spec.nodeName, startTime: .status.startTime}

view.cannot_prove: Objects are the cluster's state when the query ran, not during the incident window: they cannot prove what was true earlier, and an object missing now may have existed then. Events cover only their own timestamps inside the window; an event that is not returned is unknown, not proof nothing happened (events expire and timestamps are often null). A jq result is what the expression selected, not a full picture of the kind. When the API server returns zero objects of a kind other than events (every page read), the result is ok with total_items_processed 0: it proves only that there were no objects matching this kind, namespace and selectors at query time, not that none existed during the incident. Zero events, or a list your filter reduced to nothing, stays no_data. metadata.managedFieldsSummary gives each manager's last write time only: it is not a full change history (earlier writes by the same manager are gone) and it does not say which fields that write changed.
